A station is a block id, a `#tag` of blocks or a project block, near when it's within the recipe's `station_range` (4 by default) on every axis.

params.name: player
params.doc: Who makes them: their inventory, and where they stand.

returns.doc: In id order. Empty for a player who is offline.

functions.example:
for _, recipe in ipairs(nf.recipes.available(player)) do
  log(recipe.id .. " x" .. recipe.times)
end

functions.name: craft
functions.doc: Makes a `station` recipe for a player: takes its materials from their inventory and gives them its result (what doesn't fit drops at their feet), `times` over, or as many times as they can when that's fewer. A station it needs that isn't near makes nothing. A material matches as a recipe's ingredient does: an item id or a `#tag` takes any stack of that kind but a project item's, and a project item only its own stacks. A station is a block id, a `#tag` of blocks or a project block, near when it's within the recipe's `station_range` (4 by default) on every axis. A recipe that isn't a station one is an error.

params.name: id
params.doc: The recipe's id.

returns.doc: How many times it was made: 0 when it couldn't be, or the player is offline.

functions.example:
local made = nf.recipes.craft(player, "copper_pickaxe")
if made == 0 then
  player:send_message("<red>You can't make that here.")
end

functions.name: all
functions.doc: Every recipe's id: the project's files', then those scripts registered.

classes.name: nf.loot
classes.doc: Loot tables: the project's own (`loot/<id>.json`) and the game's. A roll picks from each of a table's pools, weighing its entries against each other, and gives the items it picked. The same `seed` always gives the same items (the editor rolls the same way). A table the project doesn't have, or that the game doesn't, is an error; so is a game table that needs something the roll doesn't say (a mob's table needs the mob, as `looted`).

functions.name: roll
functions.doc: Rolls a loot table and gives the items it picked, in the order it picked them: a stack each, more than one when a pick gives more than a stack holds. Nothing is put anywhere: give them to a player, drop them or fill a chest with them. A game table is rolled by the server where the context says (`location`, else its player's or looted entity's place), and needs one of them.

params.name: table
params.doc: A loot table of the project's (`"treasure"`, `loot/treasure.json`; a bare id is the calling package's own), one a package exports (`"acme:treasure"`), or one of the game's by its id (`"minecraft:chests/simple_dungeon"`).

params.name: context
params.doc: Who and what the roll is for: its player, tool, luck and seed. Leave it out for a roll with none of them.

functions.example:
local items = nf.loot.roll("treasure", { player = player, tool = player:equipment("main_hand") })
for _, item in ipairs(items) do
  player:inventory():add_item(item)
end

functions.name: fill
functions.doc: Rolls a loot table into an inventory the way the game fills a chest: each stack into an empty slot picked at random (from the roll's seed), leaving what's there. In a player's inventory only the hotbar and main inventory take loot. What finds no empty slot is left out. A game table is rolled where the inventory is, unless the context says otherwise.

params.name: table
params.doc: A loot table of the project's (`"treasure"`, `loot/treasure.json`; a bare id is the calling package's own), one a package exports (`"acme:treasure"`), or one of the game's by its id (`"minecraft:chests/simple_dungeon"`).

params.name: context
params.doc: Who and what the roll is for: its player, tool, luck and seed. Leave it out for a roll with none of them.

returns.doc: How many items didn't fit: 0 when all of it went in. `nil` once the inventory's gone, and then nothing is rolled.

functions.example:
local block = world:block(vec3(10, 64, 10))
local chest = block and block:inventory()
if chest then
  nf.loot.fill("treasure", chest, { luck = 1 })
end

classes.name: nf.bossbars
classes.doc: Boss bars: bars across the top of players' screens.

functions.name: create
functions.doc: Makes a boss bar, shown to no one yet (`bar:show_to(player)`). It belongs to this script and goes when it unloads. A key the options don't have is an error.
functions.example:
local bar = nf.bossbars.create({ text = "<red>The Warden", color = "red", progress = 1 })
for _, player in ipairs(nf.players.online()) do
  bar:show_to(player)
end

classes.name: nf.teams
classes.doc: The project's scoreboard teams: prefixes and suffixes on names, name colours and glow colours, friendly fire, name tags and collision.

functions.name: create
functions.doc: Makes a team on the server's scoreboard, with no members yet (`team:add_member`). It belongs to this script and goes when the script unloads, so make it in the script's body. A name that isn't letters, digits and `_`, `-`, `.` or `+`, a name one of the project's teams already has, or a key the options don't have is an error; to share a team between scripts, find it with `nf.teams.get` in the others.

params.name: name
params.doc: What the project calls it: `"red"`.

functions.name: get
functions.doc: One of the project's teams by name, or `nil` when it has none by that name.

functions.name: all
functions.doc: Every team the project has now, in the order they were made. Teams made with `/team` or by other plugins aren't among them.

classes.name: nf.schedule
classes.doc: Runs a function at a time of day, every day or week, or by a cron expression: real time, as opposed to ticks (`nf.after`, `nf.every`). Times are in the server owner's time zone (`schedules.time-zone` in `config.yml`, the server's own zone by default), not the player's. Daylight saving follows the zone's rules. A daily or weekly time the clocks skip runs the same distance after the gap begins (`"02:30"` runs at 03:30 on the day clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00), and one that happens twice runs the first time only. A cron expression matches the clock as it reads: a time the clocks skip doesn't happen that day, one for a single time of day that happens twice (`"30 1 * * *"`) runs the first time only, and one that matches every half hour keeps matching through an hour that repeats. A schedule belongs to the script that made it and ends when that script unloads (a reload, the server stopping), so the script's body makes it again. It's checked once a tick, so a callback runs within a tick (50 ms) of its time. A run the server missed (it was off at the time) is skipped, unless the schedule has `catch_up = true` and an `id`: then it runs once, on start. What a schedule last ran is kept in the server's store by `id`, per package.

functions.name: daily
functions.doc: Calls `callback` every day at a time of day. Runs on the main thread, in the tick that finds the time has come, like an `nf.every` callback. One that errors is logged with its file and line; the schedule carries on.

params.name: time
params.doc: The time of day on a 24-hour clock, `"HH:mm"`: `"18:00"`, `"06:30"`.

params.name: options
params.doc: A table: `id` (a name that survives restarts, which `catch_up` needs) and `catch_up` (run once on start if a run was missed).

functions.name: weekly
functions.doc: Calls `callback` once a week, on a day at a time of day. Runs on the main thread, in the tick that finds the time has come, like an `nf.every` callback. One that errors is logged with its file and line; the schedule carries on.

params.name: day
params.doc: The weekday: `"mon"`, `"tue"`, `"wed"`, `"thu"`, `"fri"`, `"sat"` or `"sun"` (or written out, `"saturday"`), in any case.

params.name: time
params.doc: The time of day, as for `nf.schedule.daily`.

params.name: options
params.doc: A table: `id` (a name that survives restarts, which `catch_up` needs) and `catch_up` (run once on start if a run was missed).

functions.name: cron
functions.doc: Calls `callback` whenever a cron expression matches. Runs on the main thread, in the tick that finds the time has come, like an `nf.every` callback. One that errors is logged with its file and line; the schedule carries on.

params.name: expression
params.doc: Five fields, as Unix cron has them: minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week (`0` or `7` is Sunday; `MON`-`SUN` and `JAN`-`DEC` work), each `*`, a number, a list (`1,15`), a range (`9-17`) or a step (`*/10`, `0-30/5`). `"*/30 * * * *"` is every half hour; `"0 4 * * 1-5"` is 04:00 on weekdays. An expression that isn't valid is an error.

params.name: options
params.doc: A table: `id` (a name that survives restarts, which `catch_up` needs) and `catch_up` (run once on start if a run was missed).

classes.name: nf.economy
classes.doc: Players' money, as the server's economy plugin keeps it, through [Vault](https://www.spigotmc.org/resources/vault.34315/): whichever economy is registered with it (EssentialsX, CMI, …) answers, so a project never names one. Needs Vault and an economy plugin. The plugin has to be on the server and enabled: a package that declares it (`requires`) while it isn't is a problem on the project's problem list until it is, and calling without it is an error. A plugin that is enabled after NetherForge counts from then on. The economy is looked up when it's asked, so one that registers late (after NetherForge starts) works from then on. Amounts are plain numbers in the economy's own currency; a player who is offline works as well as one who is online.

functions.name: balance
functions.doc: How much money the player has: `0` for someone the economy has no account for.

params.name: player
params.doc: Online or not.

functions.example: player:send_message("You have " .. nf.economy.balance(player) .. " coins")

functions.name: deposit
functions.doc: Gives the player money. Returns their new balance, or `nil` when the economy refused (it has no account for them, or can't hold that much). An amount that isn't positive and finite is an error.

params.name: player
params.doc: Online or not.

params.name: amount
params.doc: More than 0.

returns.doc: their balance afterwards

functions.example:
local balance = nf.economy.deposit(player, 50)
if balance then
  player:send_message("Paid out. You have " .. balance)
end

functions.name: withdraw
functions.doc: Takes money from the player. Returns their new balance, or `nil` when the economy refused, usually because they don't have that much (nothing is taken then). An amount that isn't positive and finite is an error.

params.name: player
params.doc: Online or not.

params.name: amount
params.doc: More than 0.

returns.doc: their balance afterwards

functions.example:
if nf.economy.withdraw(player, 100) then
  player:send_message("<green>Bought")
else
  player:send_message("<red>You can't afford that")
end

classes.name: nf.placeholders
classes.doc: Placeholders, through [PlaceholderAPI](https://www.spigotmc.org/resources/placeholderapi.6245/): fill in the `%player_name%`-style placeholders every plugin offers, and offer your own as `%<namespace>_<key>%` to every plugin that reads them (scoreboards, chat formats, holograms). Needs PlaceholderAPI. The plugin has to be on the server and enabled: a package that declares it (`requires`) while it isn't is a problem on the project's problem list until it is, and calling without it is an error. A plugin that is enabled after NetherForge counts from then on.

functions.name: parse
functions.doc: Replaces every placeholder in the text with its value, as PlaceholderAPI does: `"Hello %player_name%"` becomes `"Hello Alex"`. A placeholder nobody answers is left as written. Placeholders registered with `nf.placeholders.register` are answered too. A value is plain text, not MiniMessage: if it comes from players, `nf.text.escape` the result before sending it as MiniMessage.

params.name: text
params.doc: Text with `%placeholders%` in it.

params.name: player
params.doc: Whom the placeholders are about (`%player_name%`); without one, only placeholders that don't need a player have a value.

functions.example:
local line = nf.placeholders.parse("Welcome, %player_name%! Rank: %vault_rank%", player)
player:send_message(nf.text.escape(line))

functions.name: register
functions.doc: Makes `%<namespace>_<key>%` a placeholder for the whole server: PlaceholderAPI asks `callback` for the value whenever any plugin parses it. `callback` is called with the `key` (everything after the first `_`, so `%shop_price_apple%` is `"price_apple"`) and the player it's for, if there is one, and returns the text (or a number) to put there, or `nil` when it has no value for that key (the placeholder is then left as written). It runs on the main thread when the server asks from the main thread; PlaceholderAPI is also asked from other threads (async chat, scoreboard plugins), where scripts can't run: there the placeholder answers the value `callback` last gave for that same key and player, and `nil` before it ever has. The placeholder belongs to the script that registered it and goes when that script unloads (a reload, the server stopping). A namespace another script or plugin already uses is an error.

params.name: namespace
params.doc: What comes before the first `_`: lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter, at most 32 characters, like `"shop"`.

params.name: callback
params.doc: Gives the value. An error in it is logged with its file and line, and the placeholder is left as written for that request.

functions.example:
nf.placeholders.register("shop", function(key, player)
  if key == "sales" then
    return nf.data("shop").sales or 0
  end
  return nil
end)
-- %shop_sales% now works in any plugin that reads placeholders

classes.name: nf.particles
classes.doc: The project's particle effects (`particles/<id>/effect.json`): timelines of particles authored in the editor, played at a place by scripts.

functions.name: play
functions.doc: Starts playing an effect at a place, from its first tick. It plays for its `duration` (or, looping, until it's stopped) and belongs to the script that played it: when that script unloads, the effect ends (reason `"unloaded"`). Only players within 32 blocks see it (128 for an emitter with `force`), and of those only `viewers` when given. An effect the project doesn't have, a key `options` doesn't take, or an option out of range is an error, and so is an effect whose file has errors and never had a good version (one that did plays its last good version). More than 1024 effects playing on the server at once is an error too: stop the ones you're done with.

params.name: effect
params.doc: Which effect: its folder name under `particles/`.

params.name: location_or_position
params.doc: Where it plays: a `Location`, whose `yaw` and `pitch` turn the effect (nil is 0), or a position in the calling centity's world (the server's first world, in a module or a menu or dialog script).

params.name: options
params.doc: Who sees it, how big it is, whether it loops, and what it follows.

returns.doc: The playing effect, or `nil` when the world isn't loaded.

functions.example:
assert(this:node("lid")):on("click", function(event)
  nf.task(function()
    local here = this:location()
    local effect = here and nf.particles.play("shockwave", here)
    if effect then
      nf.wait_for(effect, "end")
    end
    this:play_animation("open")
  end)
  event:stop()
end)

classes.name: nf.cutscenes
classes.doc: The project's cutscenes (`cutscenes/<id>.json`): camera paths keyed in the editor, played for one player at a time.

functions.name: play
functions.doc: Starts a cutscene for a player, from its first moment. While it plays, the player spectates a camera that follows the cutscene's path, and can't move or interact. Their game mode, position, flying state and anything riding are put back when it ends, however it ends (including when they leave, a reload or the server stopping); someone who was riding something is dismounted and isn't put back on it. The camera's chunk is kept loaded while it's there, so a path may start and go anywhere in the world, however far from the player. It belongs to the script that played it: when that script unloads, it ends (reason `"unloaded"`). A player who is already watching one has it end (reason `"replaced"`) and the new one start without putting them back first, so cutscenes chain without a flash of the world they were in. A cutscene the project doesn't have, a key `options` doesn't take, or one whose file has errors and never had a good version (one that did plays its last good version) is an error. A player who is offline, or a dead one, gets `nil`.

params.name: player
params.doc: Who watches.

params.name: cutscene
params.doc: Which cutscene: its file name under `cutscenes/`, without `.json`.

params.name: options
params.doc: Where the path is, and whether the player may skip it.

returns.doc: The playing cutscene, or `nil` when the player can't watch one.

functions.example:
nf.commands.register("intro", { players_only = true }, function(event)
  local player = assert(event.player)
  local intro = nf.cutscenes.play(player, "intro", { origin = player:location() })
  if intro then
    intro:on("end", function(done)
      done.player:send_message("<gold>Welcome to the village!")
    end)
  end
end)

functions.name: stop
functions.doc: Ends the cutscene a player is watching now, with reason `"stopped"`, and puts them back.

params.name: player
params.doc: Whose cutscene to end.

returns.doc: `false` when they were not watching one.

functions.name: current
functions.doc: The cutscene a player is watching now.

params.name: player
params.doc: Who.

returns.doc: `nil` when they are not watching one.

classes.name: nf.screens
classes.doc: Screens: walls of maps, 128 by 128 pixels each, that scripts draw on (pixels, shapes, text, pictures) and play videos on. The project's own are its `screens/<id>/screen.json` files; a script can make more. What a screen shows is sent to each player who can see it, a change at a time, so drawing every tick costs only what changed.

functions.name: get
functions.doc: One of the project's screens (`screens/<id>/screen.json`). A screen the project doesn't have, or one whose file has errors and never had a good version, is an error.

params.name: screen
params.doc: Its folder name under `screens/`.

functions.example:
local board = nf.screens.get("lobby_board")
board:clear("#101018")

functions.name: all
functions.doc: Every one of the project's screens, and every screen a script made that's still there.

functions.name: create
functions.doc: Makes a screen. It belongs to the script that made it: when that script unloads, the screen goes, its frames taken down. With a `key`, the screen's maps keep their numbers for good (a map item handed out, or a frame someone hung, still shows it after a restart, once a script makes it again with the same key); without one, they're new each time. A size outside 1 to 16 maps is an error.

params.name: options
params.doc: Its size, and how it shows.

functions.example:
local scores = nf.screens.create({ width = 3, height = 2, key = "scores" })
scores:place(nf.worlds.default():location(vec3(10, 70, -4)), "south")
scores:text(8, 8, "<gold>Top players")

functions.name: fonts
functions.doc: The fonts text can be drawn in: `default` (the game's own map font) and every font of the project's (`screen_fonts/<id>/`).

functions.name: measure_text
functions.doc: How big `text` would be drawn with `options`, in pixels, without drawing it. An unknown font is an error.

params.name: text
params.doc: MiniMessage: colours and `<b>`, `<u>`, `<st>` are drawn.

params.name: options
params.doc: How it would be drawn.

functions.name: map_color
functions.doc: The colour a map would really draw for `color`: the nearest it can show, as `#rrggbb`, or `"clear"` for `"clear"`. A colour that isn't written `#rrggbb` is an error.

params.name: color
params.doc: A colour, `#rrggbb` (drawn as the nearest of the colours a map can show), or `"clear"` for none: the map shows through.

functions.example: print(nf.screens.map_color("#ff8800")) -- the orange a map really shows

functions.name: looking_at
functions.doc: The screen a player is looking at and the pixel at the middle of their view, within `distance` blocks; `nil` when they look at none, or something solid is in the way. Screens hidden from the player are looked through.

params.name: player
params.doc: Who.

params.name: distance
params.doc: How far to look, in blocks (default 64).

classes.name: nf.files
classes.doc: Files in the one directory scripts may keep things in: the only state a script has that survives a restart.

functions.name: get
functions.doc: A file or folder in the data directory, which survives restarts and reloads. A handle is a path, not an open file: nothing is read until you ask. Paths that would leave that directory (`..`, backslashes, names starting with a dot) give `nil` rather than an error. No argument is the directory itself.

params.name: path
params.doc: Relative, with `/` between folders.

functions.example:
local save = assert(nf.files.get("scores.json"))
local scores = save:read_json() or {}
scores[player:name()] = (scores[player:name()] or 0) + 1
save:write_json(scores)

classes.name: nf.text
classes.doc: Helpers for the MiniMessage text players see: escaping what players typed, stripping tags, resource pack glyphs, moving the cursor, and measuring.

functions.name: escape
functions.doc: Escapes text so MiniMessage shows it as typed rather than reading tags in it. Use it on anything a player wrote (a name they chose, a dialog answer, a chat line) before putting it into MiniMessage: otherwise they can add colours, or worse, `<click:run_command:...>`.

params.name: text
params.doc: Plain text.

returns.doc: MiniMessage that reads as exactly that text.

functions.example: player:send_message("<green>Hello, " .. nf.text.escape(tostring(event.values.nickname)))

functions.name: strip
functions.doc: MiniMessage with its tags taken out: the plain text a player would read, for logs and comparisons.

params.name: text
params.doc: MiniMessage.

functions.name: glyph
functions.doc: The character a resource pack glyph is drawn as, for building text by hand: a glyph wider than 256 pixels is drawn in pieces, so it's those pieces' characters and the moves between them. In MiniMessage text the tag `<glyph:ui/coin>` is usually simpler: it works anywhere text does (names, lore, chat, titles, dialogs, text displays) and draws the picture in its own colours, never bold, while this text is tinted by the text colour around it like any other (wrap it in `<white>` to avoid that, and keep it out of `<bold>`, which pulls a wide glyph's pieces apart). `nil` while the project's resource packs have errors (nothing is built then); a glyph no resource pack has is an error.

params.name: glyph
params.doc: `<pack>/<key>`, like `"ui/coin"`, or another loaded package's as `<namespace>:<pack>/<key>` ([looks are values](packages.md#looks-are-values)).

functions.example:
local coin = nf.text.glyph("ui/coin")
player:send_message("<white>" .. coin .. "</white> <gold>" .. balance)

functions.name: space
functions.doc: Characters that move the cursor `pixels` GUI pixels (negative is left) and draw nothing, for building text by hand: what the tag `<space:N>` inserts. In MiniMessage the tag is usually simpler, and `<at:N>…</at>` draws something N pixels away without moving what follows (`<at:-30><glyph:ui/head></at>King Slime`; add `from=center`, `from=start` or `from=end` to count N from the middle, start or end of the line, and `align=right` or `align=center` to put that edge of what it holds there). The characters are the resource pack's, so they need one: `nil` while there's none (the project has no resource packs or blocks). Inside `<bold>` each character is a pixel wider, which the tag isn't. Held to ±2047.

params.name: pixels
params.doc: How far, in GUI pixels.

functions.example:
local column = nf.text.width("Sword") or 0
player:send_message("Sword" .. (nf.text.space(60 - column) or " ") .. "<gold>12 gold")

functions.name: width
functions.doc: How wide a line of MiniMessage text draws in the game's default font, in pixels (GUI pixels: the font is 8 tall), for laying out menu titles and text displays. Tags draw nothing, except `<bold>` (a pixel more per character), `<glyph:ui/coin>` (the glyph's own width) and `<space:N>` (N, which may be negative); what an `<at:N>` holds takes no width. Text with line breaks measures as its widest line. It reads the default font's widths from `fonts/default.json`, which the editor writes into the project from your Minecraft install. `nil` when it can't be measured exactly: that file is missing (open the project in the editor with Minecraft imported), or the text uses a character it doesn't cover.

params.name: text
params.doc: MiniMessage.

functions.example:
local width = nf.text.width("<bold>Shop")
if width then
  log("the title is " .. width .. " pixels wide")
end

classes.name: nf.looks
classes.doc: Resource pack looks (item models, glyphs, skins, tooltips, equipment looks, sounds) handed from one package's code to another's. A look is a value, not a use: any script can show any look the server has, by its full name `<namespace>:<pack>/<key>`, whether or not its package exports it or is one the script's package depends on. That's how a project hands a package it uses looks of its own to draw with (see [Packages](packages.md#looks-are-values)).

functions.name: qualify
functions.doc: A look's full name, `<namespace>:<pack>/<key>`, as the calling script's package names it: `"nether/pawn"` in the project `chess_server` is `"chess_server:nether/pawn"`, which means the same in any package's code. Hand that to a package, never the bare name: a bare name means the package's own look wherever it's used. A name that already has a namespace comes back as it is. It's a plain string, so it can be kept in saved data (`this:data()`). Whether the look is there isn't checked here, but where it's shown; a name that isn't shaped like a look is an error.

params.name: look
params.doc: `<pack>/<key>`, or `<namespace>:<pack>/<key>`.

classes.name: nf.json
classes.doc: JSON text to and from Lua values.

functions.name: encode
functions.doc: A value as JSON text, written the way a `data()` table is saved: tables numbered from 1 become arrays, other tables objects (with string keys, in order), and the API's own values one-key objects that `nf.json.decode` turns back into them: `vec3(1, 2, 3)` is `{"$vec3":[1,2,3]}`, and `Location`s and `Player`, `Entity`, `Centity` and `World` handles have tags of their own. A key of yours that would read as a tag (`"$vec3"`) is written with one more `$`; any other key (`"$ref"`) is written as it is. A value JSON can't hold (a function, another kind of handle, a table that contains itself, a number key outside a list) is an error naming where it was (`value.callback: a function can't be written as JSON`).
functions.example: log(nf.json.encode({ name = "crate", sizes = { 1, 2, 3 } }))

functions.name: decode
functions.doc: JSON text as a Lua value: objects and arrays become tables, and what `nf.json.encode` tags becomes a `Vec3`, `Location` or handle again. `nil` for text that isn't JSON (and for `null`), so text from a player or a file can be tried without guarding.

classes.name: nf.http
classes.doc: Requests to web services (a Discord webhook, a status API). A package declares the hosts it talks to in `netherforge.json`'s `requires` (`"http": ["discord.com"]`, or `"*.discord.com"` for every name under it), and the server owner sees every host the project and its packages declare when it starts (`/nf requires`); a request to any other host is an error. Every request is held to the package whose code makes it. The server looks a name up once, checks the addresses it leads to and connects to exactly the address it checked: a loopback, private, link-local, shared (`100.64.0.0/10`), unique-local or IPv4-mapped address is refused even when its name is declared, unless the server owner turned on `http.allow-private-addresses` in `config.yml` (for a service on the same machine or network). Redirects (at most 5) are followed, and each one is held to the same rules, host declaration included. The server's proxy settings are never used. Only `http` and `https` URLs work. The server owner also limits requests in `config.yml`'s `http:` section: how large a request and a response may be, how long a request may take, and how many a package may make a minute. Connections that stay open (`stream`, `websocket`) are held to the same hosts and addresses, count as a request when they open, and have limits of their own in `http.connections`.

functions.name: request
functions.doc: Sends an HTTP request and gives the response. Any response is a result, whatever its status: a `404` or `500` is `response.status`, not an error, so check it. `nil, err` is for a request that couldn't be made or finished: a name that doesn't resolve, an address that isn't allowed, a refused connection, a timeout, a response over the size limit, too many requests this minute, a redirect to a host the package didn't declare, or more than 5 redirects. A mistake in the call itself (a URL that isn't `http` or `https`, a host the package didn't declare, a body over the limit, a header that can't be sent) is an error at the script's line. It works off the main thread, so its response arrives later: give `callback`, which is called with `response, err` once it's done, or call it inside a task (`nf.task`) without one, and it waits and returns `response, err`. Without a callback outside a task, it's an error. When it fails, `response` is `nil` and `err` says why.

params.name: options
params.doc: The request: its `url`, and optionally its `method`, `headers` and `body`.

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called on the main thread once it's done, as this script's code, with the response: its status, headers and body (or `nil` and why not). Not called if the script has stopped by then.

functions.example:
nf.task(function()
  local response, err = nf.http.request({
    method = "POST",
    url = "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/123/token",
    headers = { ["content-type"] = "application/json" },
    body = nf.json.encode({ content = "someone joined" }),
  })
  if not response then
    log("webhook failed: " .. err)
  elseif response.status >= 400 then
    log("webhook said " .. response.status)
  end
end)

returns.doc: Only without a callback, in a task: the response: its status, headers and body, or `nil`.
Why it failed, when it did; `nil` when it worked.

functions.name: stream
functions.doc: Opens a request whose response keeps coming (an NDJSON feed, Server-Sent Events, any chunked stream) and hands it over piece by piece as the stream's `message` events, on the main thread, as the server sends it. It returns at once: the connection is made off the main thread, and its `open` event says when the response has begun (with its status, which may be an error's: check it). It ends once, with its `end` event saying why: the server finished, `close()` was called, it failed, an owner's limit was reached, nothing came for too long, or the script that opened it unloaded. Nothing reconnects by itself: open it again from `end` if you want to, waiting longer each time. Redirects are followed as for `request`. The hosts, addresses and request rules are `request`'s, and opening counts as a request against the package's rate; a mistake in the call is an error at the script's line, and a limit the owner set (too many open, the request rate) ends the stream at the next tick with reason `"limit"`.

params.name: options
params.doc: The request (`url`, and optionally `method`, `headers` and `body`) and how to split what comes back (`format`).

returns.doc: The stream: listen to its `open`, `message` and `end`.

functions.example:
local function follow()
  local feed = nf.http.stream({ url = "https://status.example.com/events", format = "events" })
  feed:on("message", function(event)
    if event.type == "incident" then
      nf.server.broadcast("<red>" .. nf.json.decode(event.data).title)
    end
  end)
  feed:on("end", function(event)
    if event.reason ~= "unloaded" then
      nf.after(20 * 30, follow)
    end
  end)
end
follow()

functions.name: websocket
functions.doc: Opens a WebSocket (a `ws://` or `wss://` URL): a connection both sides send text messages over, for as long as it stays open (a chat bridge, a game feed, Discord's gateway). It returns at once: the connection is made off the main thread, and the socket's `open` event says when it's ready (what `send` sends before then waits for it). Each text message from the other side is a `message` event on the main thread, in order. It ends once, with its `end` event saying why. Nothing reconnects by itself. The host must be one the package declares in `requires.http`, as for `request` (the same declaration covers both), and the address rules are `request`'s; redirects aren't followed. A mistake in the call is an error at the script's line, and a limit the owner set (too many open, the request rate) ends it at the next tick with reason `"limit"`.

params.name: options
params.doc: Where to connect (`url`), and optionally `headers` and the `protocols` to offer.

returns.doc: The socket: listen to its `open`, `message` and `end`, and `send` on it.

functions.example:
local socket = nf.http.websocket({ url = "wss://chat.example.com/live" })
socket:on("open", function()
  socket:send(nf.json.encode({ hello = "minecraft" }))
end)
socket:on("message", function(event)
  local said = nf.json.decode(event.data)
  nf.server.broadcast("<gray>[web] " .. said.author .. ": " .. said.text)
end)
nf.on("player_chat", function(event)
  socket:send(nf.json.encode({ author = event.player:name(), text = event.message }))
end)

classes.name: nf.web
classes.doc: Web requests to the server: webhooks from stores, CI and chat services, "log in with…" callbacks, small pages and JSON for a companion site. A package declares `"requires": { "web": true }` in its `netherforge.json`, and its routes live under its own path, `/<namespace>/`, so packages can't collide. They're served only once the server owner turns web routes on (`web.enabled` in `config.yml`), on the port the resource pack is served from, usually behind a reverse proxy that adds HTTPS; until then a package that declares them has a warning (`runtime.web-disabled`). Every request waits for the main thread: handlers run there, under the script's budget, like any handler, and the owner limits how large a request may be, how many each address may make a minute and how many may wait (`web:` in `config.yml`). `/nf requires` lists every route.

functions.name: route
functions.doc: Answers requests for `method` at `path`, under the package's own `/<namespace>/`: `nf.web.route("POST", "/hooks/store", …)` in package `shop` answers `POST /shop/hooks/store`. A segment `:name` matches any one segment and hands it over as `request.params.name`; a last segment `*name` matches the rest of the path, slashes and all. `handler` is called with the request and a response to answer it with, now (`response:send`) or later, from a task or a callback (an `nf.http.request`, a database query); one not answered within `web.handler-timeout-seconds` is answered `504`. A `GET` route answers `HEAD` too. The route belongs to the script that made it and goes when it unloads; requests still waiting then are answered `503`. Two routes of one package for the same method and path, a path that isn't one, and a path a login (`nf.web.oauth`) uses are errors.

params.name: method
params.doc: The HTTP method.

params.name: path
params.doc: Where, under the package's own path: `/` and segments of letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.` and `~`, `:name` or a last `*name`. `"/"` is the package's own path itself.

params.name: handler
params.doc: Called on the main thread with the request and the response to answer it with. An error in it answers `500` and is reported as any handler's.

returns.doc: The route: `route:remove()` stops answering.

functions.example:
nf.web.route("GET", "/players/:name", function(request, response)
  local player = nf.players.get(request.params.name)
  if not player then
    response:json(404, { error = "not online" })
    return
  end
  response:json(200, { name = player:name(), health = player:health() })
end)

functions.name: url
functions.doc: The address the world reaches the calling package's `path` at: `web.public-url` in `config.yml` (the server's own address when it's empty), then `/<namespace>`, `path` and the query. For a link to put in chat, a webhook to register with another service, a login's address. `nil` while the server owner hasn't turned web routes on.

params.name: path
params.doc: A path under the package's own, like a route's: `"/replays/12"`. Default `"/"`.

params.name: query
params.doc: Query parameters, encoded and sorted by name.

functions.example:
local link = nf.web.url("/replays/" .. replay_id)
if link then
  player:send_message("<click:open_url:" .. link .. ">Watch the replay</click>")
end

functions.name: verify_signature
functions.doc: Whether `signature` is the HMAC of `body` under `options.secret`, as webhook senders sign what they send (GitHub's `X-Hub-Signature-256`, Stripe's and Shopify's): compared in constant time, so the answer leaks nothing about the right one. Check it before acting on a webhook. Keep the secret in a setting (`nf.config`), not in a script. A signature that isn't in `options.encoding` is `false`, not an error.

params.name: body
params.doc: The request's body exactly as it came: `request.body`.

params.name: signature
params.doc: The signature the sender sent, from its header.

params.name: options
params.doc: The secret, and how the sender signs.

functions.example:
nf.web.route("POST", "/hooks/github", function(request, response)
  local signed = nf.web.verify_signature(request.body, request.headers["x-hub-signature-256"] or "", {
    secret = nf.config("github_secret"),
    prefix = "sha256=",
  })
  if not signed then
    response:send(401)
    return
  end
  response:send(204)
end)

functions.name: oauth
functions.doc: A "log in with…" flow (OAuth 2 with PKCE, the authorization code grant): `flow:begin(player)` gives the address to send the player to, the service sends them back to the flow's own route (`/<namespace>/oauth/<name>/callback`, which you register with the service as its redirect URI: `nf.web.url("/oauth/<name>/callback")`), and the server trades the code for a token itself and raises `complete` (or `fail`) on the flow. NetherForge keeps the state and the code verifier, ties each to the player who began, uses each once and lets it expire after 10 minutes, so a forged or replayed callback is refused. The token endpoint's host must be one the package declares in `requires.http`. The flow belongs to the script that made it and goes when it unloads; logins begun before a reload are forgotten. Two flows of one package with the same `name` are an error.

params.name: options
params.doc: The service's endpoints, the client's id and secret, and the scopes to ask for.

functions.example:
local discord = nf.web.oauth({
  name = "discord",
  authorize_url = "https://discord.com/oauth2/authorize",
  token_url = "https://discord.com/api/oauth2/token",
  client_id = nf.config("discord_client_id"),
  client_secret = nf.config("discord_client_secret"),
  scopes = { "identify" },
})
discord:on("complete", function(event)
  event.player:send_message("<green>Linked your Discord account")
end)
nf.commands.register("link", function(event)
  local url = event.player and discord:begin(event.player)
  if url then
    event.player:send_message("<click:open_url:" .. url .. "><u>Click to link Discord</u></click>")
  end
end)

classes.name: nf.wasm
classes.doc: Heavy computation in WebAssembly: a chess engine, pathfinding over a big grid, noise, compression, a library compiled from C, C++ or Rust. A module is `wasm/<id>/module.wasm` in the project (or a package's, exported), built for WASI preview 1 and single-threaded (`wasm32-wasip1`); every other file in its folder is data it can read, never write, as files from its root (`/`). It runs off the main thread, with no access to the server, the network or any file but its own data: it can only answer the script that asked. A package declares it runs modules with `"requires": { "wasm": true }`, and the server owner sees that (`/nf requires`) and limits it in `config.yml`'s `wasm:` section: how many threads run modules, how much memory each may use, how long a call may take, and how many instances and programs a package may keep. There are three ways to run one: `nf.wasm.instantiate` for a library whose functions you call (`instance:call`), `nf.wasm.run` for a program that reads its input and prints its answer, and `nf.wasm.start` for a program that keeps running and talks line by line (a UCI chess engine). The server compiles every module off the main thread as the project loads; one that couldn't be compiled fails when it's run, saying why (and the problem `runtime.wasm` says so too). A module the project doesn't have is an error at the script's line. A script that runs a module restarts when the module changes.

functions.name: functions
functions.doc: The functions a module exports, with their parameters' and results' types, in the order it exports them: a program (a WASI command) exports `_start`. Empty until the server has compiled it, and for one that couldn't be.

params.name: module
params.doc: Its folder name under `wasm/`, or `namespace:id` for one a package it depends on exports (see [Names across packages](packages.md)).

functions.example:
for _, fn in ipairs(nf.wasm.functions("noise")) do
  log(fn.name, table.concat(fn.params, ", "), "->", table.concat(fn.results, ", "))
end

functions.name: instantiate
functions.doc: Makes an instance of a library module: its own memory, kept between calls, which `instance:call` calls functions in. Its start function (and a reactor's `_initialize`) runs first. It fails when the module couldn't be compiled, it needs more memory than `wasm.max-memory-mb`, the server's modules together would hold more than `wasm.max-memory-total-mb`, or the package already holds `wasm.max-instances-per-package` instances. The instance belongs to the script that made it. It works off the main thread, so its instance arrives later: give `callback`, which is called with `instance, err` once it's done, or call it inside a task (`nf.task`) without one, and it waits and returns `instance, err`. Without a callback outside a task, it's an error. When it fails, `instance` is `nil` and `err` says why.

params.name: module
params.doc: Its folder name under `wasm/`, or `namespace:id` for one a package it depends on exports (see [Names across packages](packages.md)).

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called on the main thread once it's done, as this script's code, with the instance (or `nil` and why not). Not called if the script has stopped by then.

functions.example:
nf.task(function()
  local noise, err = nf.wasm.instantiate("noise")
  if not noise then
    log("no noise: " .. err)
    return
  end
  local values = noise:call("sample", { 12.5, 40.25 })
  if values then
    log("noise here:", values[1])
  end
end)

returns.doc: Only without a callback, in a task: the instance, or `nil`.
Why it failed, when it did; `nil` when it worked.

functions.name: run
functions.doc: Runs a program to its end with `options.stdin` as its input, and gives what it printed and its exit code: for a tool that reads a question and prints the answer. It's stopped (`nil, err`) past `wasm.max-call-seconds`, and what it prints is kept up to `wasm.max-output-bytes` of each stream. A program that exits with a code other than 0 has still run: check `result.exit_code`. It works off the main thread, so its result arrives later: give `callback`, which is called with `result, err` once it's done, or call it inside a task (`nf.task`) without one, and it waits and returns `result, err`. Without a callback outside a task, it's an error. When it fails, `result` is `nil` and `err` says why.

params.name: module
params.doc: Its folder name under `wasm/`, or `namespace:id` for one a package it depends on exports (see [Names across packages](packages.md)).

params.name: options
params.doc: Its input, arguments and environment.

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called on the main thread once it's done, as this script's code, with its exit code and what it printed (or `nil` and why not). Not called if the script has stopped by then.

functions.example:
nf.task(function()
  local result, err = nf.wasm.run("solver", { stdin = "3 1 2", arguments = { "--fast" } })
  if result and result.exit_code == 0 then
    log("solved:", result.stdout)
  end
end)

returns.doc: Only without a callback, in a task: its exit code and what it printed, or `nil`.
Why it failed, when it did; `nil` when it worked.

functions.name: start
functions.doc: Starts a program that keeps running: each `send` is a line of its input, each line it prints is an `output` event, on the main thread, in order, and it ends once, with its `end` event. It returns at once; the program starts off the main thread, on a thread of its own while it runs, and belongs to the script that started it. A limit the owner set (`wasm.max-processes-per-package`, `wasm.max-processes-total`, memory) ends it at the next tick with reason `"limit"`; a module that couldn't be compiled ends it `"failed"`.

params.name: module
params.doc: Its folder name under `wasm/`, or `namespace:id` for one a package it depends on exports (see [Names across packages](packages.md)).

params.name: options
params.doc: Its arguments and environment.

returns.doc: The program: listen to its `output` and `end`, and `send` it lines.

functions.example:
local engine = nf.wasm.start("stockfish")
engine:on("output", function(event)
  local move = event.line:match("^bestmove (%S+)")
  if move then
    nf.server.broadcast("The engine plays " .. move)
  end
end)
engine:send("position startpos moves e2e4")
engine:send("go movetime 1000")

classes.name: nf.network
classes.doc: The other servers of the network this one is part of: a proxy (Velocity) running NetherForge's proxy plugin, which is the network's hub, and the servers behind it, each running NetherForge and connected to the hub (`network:` in their `config.yml`). Scripts publish messages on channels every server can listen to (`nf.network.channel`), ask one server and get its answer (`channel:request`), keep values every server sees in shared maps (`nf.network.map`), know who's online on which server (`players`, the `network_player_*` events), and send a player to another server with data that arrives with them (`send_player`). A package declares it with `"requires": { "network": true }`, and the server owner sees that (`/nf requires`). Channels and maps are named in the calling package's namespace, so packages never see each other's unless one depends on the other. Everything goes through the hub: a server that isn't connected (`is_connected()`) misses what's published meanwhile, and what it sends returns `false` or fails. Delivery is at most once, and in order between any two servers. On the editor's dev server, unless its `config.yml` puts it in a network, the server is a network of its own, named `"dev"`, so channels and maps work there with no proxy (sending players doesn't). A server whose owner hasn't put it in a network has none: its packages that declare it have the warning `runtime.network-disabled`.

functions.name: server_name
functions.doc: This server's name in the network, as the proxy names it (`network.server-name` in `config.yml`); `"dev"` on the editor's dev server when it's a network of its own, `"test"` in a script test. `nil` on a server that isn't part of a network.

functions.name: is_connected
functions.doc: Whether this server is connected to its network's hub now. `network_connect` and `network_disconnect` say when that changes.

functions.name: servers
functions.doc: Every server of the network, as the proxy names them, with whether NetherForge on each is connected and how many players are on it. Empty while this server isn't connected.
functions.example:
for _, server in ipairs(nf.network.servers()) do
  log(server.name, server.connected and "up" or "down", server.players .. " online")
end

functions.name: players
functions.doc: Everyone online in the network, on any server, this one included, as the proxy last said. Empty while this server isn't connected.

functions.name: find_player
functions.doc: A player online anywhere in the network, by name (any case) or UUID; `nil` when nobody by that name or UUID is.

params.name: player
params.doc: Their name, or their UUID as a string.

functions.example:
local friend = nf.network.find_player("Ann")
if friend then
  player:send_message("Ann is on " .. friend.server)
end

functions.name: channel
functions.doc: A channel: what's `publish`ed on it reaches every server whose scripts listen to its `message` event (this one included), and a `request` on it reaches one server's `request` handlers. Getting it subscribes nothing: a server hears a channel's messages while any of its scripts has a handler on it.

params.name: name
params.doc: Its name: lowercase letters, digits and `_ . - /`, at most 64 characters. It's the calling package's own (`shop` names `"sales"` `shop:sales`), so packages can't collide; `namespace:name` names one of a package it depends on.

functions.example:
local chat = nf.network.channel("chat")
chat:on("message", function(event)
  nf.server.broadcast("<gray>[" .. event.server .. "]</gray> " .. event.value.text)
end)
nf.on("player_chat", function(event)
  chat:publish({ text = event.player:name() .. ": " .. event.message })
end)

functions.name: map
functions.doc: A shared map: keys (strings) and values the hub keeps for the whole network, which every server reads at once from its own copy and writes through the hub. The hub saves them, so they outlive any server and the proxy restarting. This server keeps a copy from the first time any script gets the map until the project reloads: `is_ready()` once the hub has sent it, and `change` events after.

params.name: name
params.doc: Its name: lowercase letters, digits and `_ . - /`, at most 64 characters. It's the calling package's own (`shop` names `"sales"` `shop:sales`), so packages can't collide; `namespace:name` names one of a package it depends on.

functions.name: send_player
functions.doc: Sends a player to another server of the network, through the proxy, with `data` for that server's scripts: its `player_arrive` handlers hear it once they've joined there. The player may be on any server, this one or another. It fails (`nil, err`) when this server isn't connected, the player isn't online, the proxy has no such server, they're already there, or the proxy couldn't move them (the server is down or full, a proxy plugin cancelled it). It works off the main thread, so its moved arrives later: give `callback`, which is called with `moved, err` once it's done, or call it inside a task (`nf.task`) without one, and it waits and returns `moved, err`. Without a callback outside a task, it's an error. When it fails, `moved` is `nil` and `err` says why.

params.name: player
params.doc: Who: a player on this server, or anyone online in the network by name or UUID.

params.name: server
params.doc: The server's name in the network, as the proxy names it (`"lobby"`); `nf.network.servers()` lists them.

params.name: data
params.doc: What arrives with them, as `event.data` there. Anything a `data()` table can hold, sent as JSON with the same codec: tables, strings, numbers, booleans, `Vec3`, `Location` (its world by name) and handles to entities and worlds (by UUID and name, which another server may not have). At most `max-value-bytes` as JSON (the proxy's `hub.properties`, 64 KiB unless its owner says otherwise); a value over it, or one that can't be written as JSON, is an error at the script's line.

params.name: callback
params.doc: Called on the main thread once it's done, as this script's code, with `true` once they are on their way there (or `nil` and why not). Not called if the script has stopped by then.

functions.example:
nf.task(function()
  local moved, err = nf.network.send_player(player, "arena", { team = "red" })
  if not moved then
    player:send_message("<red>Can't go: " .. err)
  end
end)

returns.doc: Only without a callback, in a task: `true` once they are on their way there, or `nil`.
Why it failed, when it did; `nil` when it worked.

classes.name: nf.time
classes.doc: Dates and durations as text, in the same unit as `nf.server.unix_time()`: milliseconds. For timers, use ticks (`nf.after`, `nf.wait`); this is for showing and reading clock times and lengths of time.

functions.name: format
functions.doc: A moment as clock time, in English, written the way a pattern says.

params.name: time
params.doc: Milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, like `nf.server.unix_time()` returns.

params.name: pattern
params.doc: Letters stand for parts of the date: `yyyy` the year, `MM` the month as a number (`MMM` `Oct`, `MMMM` `October`), `dd` the day, `EEE` the weekday (`Sat`; `EEEE` `Saturday`), `HH` the hour from 00 to 23 (`hh` 01 to 12, with `a` for AM or PM), `mm` minutes, `ss` seconds, `XXX` the zone's offset (`+01:00`, or `Z`). Text in single quotes is kept as it is (`'at'`); punctuation and spaces needn't be. A letter that isn't a pattern letter is an error.

functions.example:
local now = nf.server.unix_time()
player:send_message("It's " .. nf.time.format(now, "EEEE, d MMMM 'at' HH:mm", { zone = "UTC" }) .. " UTC")

functions.name: parse
functions.doc: Reads a clock time written the way a pattern says, as milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC. A pattern with no time of day reads as midnight; one with an offset (`XXX`) in it uses the offset it reads rather than `zone`. `nil` when the text doesn't match the pattern (it may come from a player); a pattern without a year, month and day, or with a letter that isn't a pattern letter, is an error.

params.name: pattern
params.doc: As for `nf.time.format`.

functions.example:
local start = nf.time.parse("2026-10-31 20:00", "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm", { zone = "Europe/London" })
if start and nf.server.unix_time() >= start then
  nf.server.broadcast("<gold>The event has begun!")
end

functions.name: duration
functions.doc: A length of time as short text, largest unit first and units that are 0 left out: `"1h 2m 5s"`, `"3d 4h"`, `"45s"`. Less than a second is `"0s"`; a negative length starts with `-`.

params.name: milliseconds
params.doc: How long.

functions.example:
local left = saved.ends_at - nf.server.unix_time()
player:send_message("Ends in " .. nf.time.duration(left))

functions.name: parse_duration
functions.doc: Reads a length of time written as numbers with units, as milliseconds: `"1h30m"`, `"1h 30m"`, `"90s"`, `"2d"`, `"1.5h"`, `"250ms"`. The units are `d`, `h`, `m`, `s` and `ms`, in any order, each at most once; spaces between them are fine. `nil` for text that isn't a duration (it may come from a player).
functions.example:
local cooldown = nf.time.parse_duration(event.arguments.cooldown)
if not cooldown then
  event.sender:send_message("<red>Try something like 10m or 1h30m")
end

classes.name: nf.random
classes.doc: Randomness `math.random` doesn't give: generators of your own that repeat for a seed, smooth noise, and random ids.

functions.name: new
functions.doc: A random generator of its own, apart from `math.random` and every other generator. Two made with the same seed give the same numbers in the same order, on every server, so a seed can stand for a whole dungeon layout or loot roll. One the script lets go of is collected like any table.

params.name: seed
params.doc: Leave it out for a generator seeded at random.

functions.example:
local rng = nf.random.new(42)
local roll = rng:integer(1, 6)
local prize = rng:weighted({ diamond = 1, iron_ingot = 5, bread = 20 })

functions.name: noise2
functions.doc: Smooth 2D noise (simplex): a number from -1 to 1 that changes gradually as `x` and `z` do, the same every time for the same arguments. For terrain heights, patches of blocks, wobble over time.
functions.example:
for x = 0, 31 do
  for z = 0, 31 do
    local height = 64 + math.floor(nf.random.noise2(x, z, { seed = 7, scale = 0.05 }) * 6)
    world:block(vec3(x, height, z)):set_state("minecraft:grass_block")
  end
end

functions.name: noise3
functions.doc: Smooth 3D noise (simplex), like `noise2` with a third coordinate: caves, clouds, or 2D noise that drifts over time (`y` as the tick).

functions.name: uuid
functions.doc: A new random UUID, like `"3f2b8c1e-7a4d-4e0b-9c55-0e8a6f1d2b7c"`: an id no one else will make.

classes.name: nf.math
classes.doc: Small arithmetic `math` doesn't have, for animating by hand: blending, clamping, rescaling and easing.

functions.name: lerp
functions.doc: The number `fraction` of the way from `from` to `to`: 0 is `from`, 1 is `to`, and outside that it carries on past either end. (`Vec3` has its own `lerp`.)

functions.name: clamp
functions.doc: `value`, kept from `min` to `max`. `min` greater than `max` is an error.

functions.name: remap
functions.doc: Moves `value` from one range to another: `from_min` becomes `to_min`, `from_max` becomes `to_max`, and everything else in proportion (beyond the ends too; clamp it if it mustn't). A range from a number to itself is an error.
functions.example: local pitch = nf.math.remap(health, 0, 20, 0.5, 2)

functions.name: ease
functions.doc: Reshapes a fraction from 0 to 1 by one of the curves animation keyframes use: `"linear"` as it is, `"step"` 0 until 1, `"ease_in"` starting slow, `"ease_out"` ending slow, `"ease_in_out"` both. Every curve takes 0 to 0 and 1 to 1; a fraction outside 0 to 1 is clamped first.

params.name: easing
params.doc: Which curve.

params.name: fraction
params.doc: How far along, 0 to 1.

functions.example:
nf.task(function()
  for tick = 0, 20 do
    local t = nf.math.ease("ease_in_out", tick / 20)
    node:set_translation(vec3(0, nf.math.lerp(0, 3, t), 0))
    nf.wait(1)
  end
end)

classes.name: nf.test
classes.doc: What a test file runs on. A project's tests are the `*_test.lua` files anywhere in it (`tests/shop_test.lua`), run by `netherforge test` (or the editor's Run tests) on a fake server: no Minecraft, no network, a world that holds only what the test puts in it. A test file runs like a module (it can `require` the project's modules, and files beside it) and registers its tests with `nf.test.case`; each test runs alone, on a fresh server with the project loaded and its scripts started, so one can never leave something behind for the next. The file's own code runs once for every test, before it, so it's where to `require` and build what the tests share. Nothing here exists on a real server: `nf.test` is `nil` there.

functions.name: case
functions.doc: Registers a test. It passes when `callback` returns, and fails at the line where an `assert` or `error` in it (or in something it calls) went wrong. A script of the project that errors while the test runs fails it too, naming that script and line. Two tests in one file can't have the same name.

params.name: name
params.doc: What the test checks, as a sentence: `"greets a new player"`.

params.name: callback
params.doc: The test. It runs synchronously: `nf.test.advance` is how time passes in it.

functions.example:
nf.test.case("a player joining is greeted", function()
  local alex = nf.test.player("Alex")
  nf.test.advance(1)
  assert(alex:name() == "Alex")
end)

functions.name: advance
functions.doc: Runs the server forward `ticks` ticks (20 are a second), whole ticks at a time: timers fall due, `tick` handlers run, centities tick and mobs think, exactly as on a server, and everything scripts started on other threads finishes first. When it returns, the last tick is done. Each call in those ticks (a handler, a timer, a centity's tick) has its own budget and time limit, as on a server: none of it counts against the test's own, which is for the test's code. One that runs out is reported as on a server, at its file and line. Script errors during it are collected and fail the test when it ends.

params.name: ticks
params.doc: At least 1.

functions.example:
local count = 0
nf.every(20, function() count = count + 1 end)
nf.test.advance(60)
assert(count == 3)

functions.name: player
functions.doc: Joins a fake player and returns them: the server raises the join events (`player_join`) as it does for a real one, and the player can then be sent messages, given items, moved and clicked at like any other `Player`. Names are unique: a name already joined gives that player.

params.name: name
params.doc: Their name, 3 to 16 letters, digits and `_`: `"Alex"`.

functions.example:
local alex = nf.test.player("Alex")
alex:send_message("<green>hi")
assert(alex:name() == "Alex")

functions.name: raise
functions.doc: Raises a server-wide event as the server would, to the scripts: whoever listens to `event` with `nf.on` hears it, and, for an event the server raises about a player, an entity or a world, the handlers on that handle (`player:on("chat")`) hear it first, in the order the server uses. Each can `stop()` or `cancel()` it or set its writable fields. The few events the runtime stages itself (a death, damage, a click on a centity) reach `nf.on` handlers only. `payload` is what the event carries, the same table its handlers read (`event.player`, `event.message`): a field the event does not have is an error naming the fields. What the server would then do with a cancelled event is not simulated: read the result.

params.name: event
params.doc: The event's name, as `nf.on` takes it.

params.name: payload
params.doc: The payload: its fields by name. Leave it out for an event that has none.

returns.doc: Whether a handler cancelled it, and the event as the handlers left it.

functions.example:
local alex = nf.test.player("Alex")
local result = nf.test.raise("player_chat", { player = alex, message = "hello", format = "<message>" })
assert(not result.cancelled)
assert(result.event.message == "hello")

functions.name: terrain
functions.doc: A stand-in for a terrain script's `terrain` (what its `...` is), to test worldgen modules on their own: `noise(name):at(...)`, `height`, `area`, `biome`, `seed`, `min_y`, `max_y`, `sea_level` and `plan` as a terrain script has them, each answering what `options` says. `noises` maps a noise's name to its value everywhere, or to a function of the place (`x, y, z`, or `x, z` for a column) giving it; a noise it doesn't name is 0. `height`, `area` and `biome` are a value or a function of the place, `seed`, `min_y`, `max_y` and `sea_level` numbers (defaults 64, `"default"`, `minecraft:plains`, 0, -64, 319 and 63). A plan makes each cell once, with `math.random` seeded for that cell. Chunks, structures and scatters aren't stood in for: `netherforge preview` draws the real thing.
functions.example:
local landforms = require("worldgen.landforms")
nf.test.case("the spawn is a meadow", function()
  landforms.init(nf.test.terrain({ noises = { ranges = 0.9 }, height = 70 }))
  assert(landforms.kind(0, 0) == "plains")
end)

functions.name: click
functions.doc: Clicks for a player as their client would, with what they hold filled in, and raises what the server would for it: `player_interact` (the held project item's `interact` first, and a click on one of the project's blocks reaches it), then, for a right click with an item that nothing cancelled, `player_use_item` (the project item's `use` first). A left click is the attack button at a block or the air: it doesn't break the block (`world:break_block` does that). A click on an entity is `nf.test.raise("player_interact_entity", ...)`. Nothing the game would then do (an item thrown, a door opened) is simulated: read what the handlers did.

params.name: player
params.doc: Who clicks: one online, from `nf.test.player`.

params.name: button
params.doc: Which button: `"right"` uses what they hold.

params.name: options
params.doc: Which hand, and the block clicked. Leave it out for the main hand at the air.

returns.doc: `true` when it went through, `false` when a handler cancelled it.

functions.example:
local alex = nf.test.player("Alex")
alex:set_held_item({ kind = "minecraft:ender_pearl" })
assert(nf.test.click(alex, "right"))

functions.name: release
functions.doc: Lets go of the right button for a player who was using an item (drawing a bow, raising a shield, eating) before it finished, as their client would: raises `player_stop_using_item` with the item in their main hand, or in their off hand when the main one is empty. Like the server, it is heard by the player before `nf.on`. An error when both hands are empty.

params.name: player
params.doc: Who lets go: one online.

params.name: ticks
params.doc: How long they held it, in ticks: a bow drawn for 20 is fully drawn. 0 or more.

functions.example:
local alex = nf.test.player("Alex")
alex:set_held_item({ kind = "minecraft:bow" })
nf.test.click(alex, "right")
nf.test.release(alex, 20)

functions.name: input
functions.doc: The movement keys a player holds now, as their client says when they change: raises `player_input` (the player's `input` first, then `nf.on`). A key left out is not held, so `nf.test.input(player, {})` lets go of every key. It only raises the event: the player doesn't move, sneak or sprint for it.

params.name: player
params.doc: Whose keys: one online.

params.name: held
params.doc: The keys held down, each `true`.

functions.example:
local alex = nf.test.player("Alex")
nf.test.input(alex, { forward = true, jump = true })

functions.name: shown
functions.doc: A stack as a player's game was last sent it, after the `view` handlers: what their tooltip says, where the server keeps the real stack (read that from `player:inventory()` or `menu:item`). The fake server sends what changed at the end of each tick, as a real one does, and what `player:refresh_items` finds looks different, so `nf.test.advance(1)` after a change. `nil` for an empty slot, or one their game hasn't been sent.

params.name: player
params.doc: Whose game: one online.

params.name: slot
params.doc: A slot of their inventory, numbered as `player:inventory()` numbers them; with `menu`, of the window they have open. `"cursor"` for the stack on their cursor.

params.name: options
params.doc: Leave it out for their own inventory.

functions.example:
local alex = nf.test.player("Alex")
alex:set_held_item(nf.items.create("ruby"))
nf.test.advance(1)
local shown = assert(nf.test.shown(alex, 0))
assert(shown.lore ~= nil)

functions.name: connections
functions.doc: The connections scripts opened with `nf.http.stream` and `nf.http.websocket` in this test, oldest first, ended ones included. In a test nothing reaches the network: each connection is held by the test, which answers it with `nf.test.accept`, talks over it with `nf.test.receive` and `nf.test.sent`, and ends it with `nf.test.disconnect`. Everything else is as on a server: the package must declare the host, the owner's limits apply (the defaults, in a test), and what the test does reaches the scripts at the next tick, so `nf.test.advance(1)` after it.

params.name: url
params.doc: Only those whose URL starts with this: `"wss://chat.example.com"`.

functions.example:
nf.test.case("the bridge says hello", function()
  require("bridge")
  local socket = nf.test.connections("wss://chat.example.com")[1] --[[@as WebSocket]]
  nf.test.accept(socket)
  nf.test.advance(1)
  assert(nf.test.sent(socket)[1] == "hello")
end)

functions.name: accept
functions.doc: Answers a connection that's still connecting, as its server would: its `open` event follows at the next tick. A stream opens with `options.status` (default `200`). Accepting one that isn't connecting any more is an error.

params.name: connection
params.doc: One from `nf.test.connections`.

params.name: options
params.doc: The status, headers and subprotocol to answer with.

functions.example:
local feed = nf.test.connections("https://feed.example.com")[1]
nf.test.accept(feed, { status = 200, headers = { ["content-type"] = "application/x-ndjson" } })

functions.name: receive
functions.doc: Sends `text` from the far end. A WebSocket hears it as one `message`; a stream reads it as more of its response, split by its `format` exactly as a server's would be (so `"a\nb\n"` is two lines, and half a line waits for the rest). It accepts a connection that's still connecting first. An error when the connection has ended, or when as many messages as `connections.max-queued-messages` are already waiting for the scripts (advance to let them in).

params.name: connection
params.doc: One from `nf.test.connections`.

params.name: text
params.doc: What the far end sends.

functions.example:
nf.test.receive(feed, '{"kind":"goal"}\n')
nf.test.advance(1)

functions.name: sent
functions.doc: Every message scripts sent on a WebSocket so far, in order, whether or not it had opened (a stream sends nothing: its request body is in its options).

params.name: connection
params.doc: One from `nf.test.connections`.

functions.name: request
functions.doc: Makes a web request to the server, as a browser or a webhook sender would, and gives its answer: it goes through the routes scripts made with `nf.web.route` and the owner's limits (the defaults, in a test) exactly as a real one does, without a network, whether or not web routes are turned on. When the handler answers later (from a task, a callback), the server runs forward tick by tick until it does, as `nf.test.advance` would, up to `web.handler-timeout-seconds` (then it's `504`).

params.name: path
params.doc: The path, namespace and all, with any query: `"/shop/replays/12?full=1"`.

params.name: options
params.doc: Its headers, body and the address it comes from.

functions.name: oauth_token
functions.doc: What a login flow's token endpoint answers in this test: in a test the server doesn't call it, and trades every code for this instead (by default `{ access_token = "test-token", token_type = "Bearer" }`). A table without `access_token` makes the login `fail`, with its `error_description` or `error`.

params.name: flow
params.doc: The flow.

params.name: response
params.doc: The token endpoint's JSON answer, as a table.

functions.example: nf.test.oauth_token(flow, { access_token = "abc", refresh_token = "def", expires_in = 3600 })

functions.name: disconnect
functions.doc: Ends a connection from the far end, after what it already received: with `options.error` it breaks (reason `"failed"`, `detail` the error), otherwise the server finishes it (`"finished"`, a WebSocket with `options.code` and `options.reason`). Its `end` event follows at the next tick. Disconnecting one that has ended does nothing.

params.name: connection
params.doc: One from `nf.test.connections`.

params.name: options
params.doc: How it ends.

functions.example:
nf.test.disconnect(socket, { code = 4000, reason = "resume" })
nf.test.advance(1)

functions.name: stub_wasm
functions.doc: Stands in for a WebAssembly module for the rest of this test, so a test needn't run a heavy one (a chess engine) to check the script around it. In a test modules really run, as on a server; once stubbed, nothing of the module runs: an instance's `call` and `call_text` answer with `stub.functions` (a function the stub doesn't have fails, `nil, err`), `run` with `stub.run`, and a program `start`ed answers each line it's sent with the lines `stub.input` returns, as `output` events at the next tick (closing its input ends it, exit code 0). Each stub function runs on the main thread as the test's code.

params.name: module
params.doc: The module, as `nf.wasm`'s functions name it.

params.name: stub
params.doc: What answers in its place.

functions.name: network_server
functions.doc: Adds another server to the test's network. In a test this server is part of a network of its own, named `"test"`, whose hub is a real one in the test: every other server is one the test adds and plays, with `network_publish`, `network_received`, `network_answer`, `network_write`, `network_join` and `network_send`. Adding one that's there does nothing; the network starts with none.

params.name: name
params.doc: Its name in the network (`"lobby"`).

functions.example:
nf.test.case("chat reaches the lobby", function()
  nf.test.network_server("lobby")
  local player = nf.test.player("Ann")
  nf.test.raise("player_chat", { player = player, message = "hi", format = "" })
  nf.test.advance(1)
  local said = nf.test.network_received("lobby", "chat")
  assert(said[1].value.text == "Ann: hi")
end)

functions.name: network_publish
functions.doc: Another server publishes `value` on a channel, to every server listening: this one's `message` handlers hear it at the next tick (`nf.test.advance(1)`).

params.name: server
params.doc: The other server's name, as `nf.test.network_server` added it.

params.name: channel
params.doc: The channel's name, as `nf.network.channel` takes it.

params.name: value
params.doc: What it publishes.

functions.name: network_received
functions.doc: What another server has heard of this test's network so far: every message published on a channel it listens to (it listens to every channel `network_received` or `network_answer` named for it, from when it's named), oldest first.

params.name: server
params.doc: The other server's name, as `nf.test.network_server` added it.

params.name: channel
params.doc: Only this channel's, by its name as `nf.network.channel` takes it; every channel's it listens to when left out.

functions.name: network_answer
functions.doc: How another server answers requests on a channel: `callback` gets what it was asked and who asked, and returns the answer (an error in it is the asker's `err`). Requests are answered at the next tick, as a real server's would be.

params.name: server
params.doc: The other server's name, as `nf.test.network_server` added it.

params.name: channel
params.doc: The channel's name, as `nf.network.channel` takes it.

params.name: callback
params.doc: Gets the request and the asking server; returns the answer.

functions.example:
nf.test.network_server("bank")
nf.test.network_answer("bank", "balance", function(name)
  return name == "Ann" and 100 or 0
end)

functions.name: network_request
functions.doc: Another server asks this one on a channel, as `channel:request` there would, and gives this server's answer: the server runs forward tick by tick until its `request` handlers have answered (they answer the tick after, as a real server's would). A request that fails (nothing here handles requests on the channel, a handler errored) is an error at the test's line, saying why.

params.name: server
params.doc: The other server's name, as `nf.test.network_server` added it.

params.name: channel
params.doc: The channel's name, as `nf.network.channel` takes it.

params.name: value
params.doc: What it asks with: the handlers read it as `event.value`.

returns.doc: What this server's handlers assigned to `event.reply`.

functions.example:
nf.test.case("the shop quotes prices to the lobby", function()
  nf.test.network_server("lobby")
  assert(nf.test.network_request("lobby", "prices", "diamond") == 42)
end)

functions.name: network_write
functions.doc: Another server sets a key of a shared map (`nil` deletes it): every server with the map hears its `change` at the next tick.

params.name: server
params.doc: The other server's name, as `nf.test.network_server` added it.

params.name: map
params.doc: The map's name, as `nf.network.map` takes it.

params.name: key
params.doc: The key.

params.name: value
params.doc: Its value, or `nil` to delete it.

functions.name: network_join
functions.doc: A player joins the network on another server, as the proxy would say: `nf.network.players()` lists them and `network_player_join` is heard at the next tick. Joining them on a server they're not on moves them there (`network_player_switch`). A player on this server is joined with `nf.test.player`, which the network hears of too.

params.name: server
params.doc: The other server's name, as `nf.test.network_server` added it.

params.name: name
params.doc: The player's name: their UUID is worked out from it, as `nf.test.player`'s is.

functions.name: network_quit
functions.doc: A player on another server leaves the network: `network_player_quit` is heard at the next tick.

params.name: name
params.doc: The player's name.

functions.name: network_send
functions.doc: Another server sends a player here with `data`, as `nf.network.send_player` there would: they join this server (`player_join`) and, the tick after, its `player_arrive` handlers hear `data`. They needn't be in the network yet.

params.name: server
params.doc: The other server's name, as `nf.test.network_server` added it.

params.name: name
params.doc: The player's name.

params.name: data
params.doc: What arrives with them.

functions.example:
nf.test.case("a sent player gets their kit", function()
  nf.test.network_server("lobby")
  local player = nf.test.network_send("lobby", "Ann", { kit = "archer" })
  nf.test.advance(1)
  assert(player:inventory():count_item("minecraft:bow") == 1)
end)

classes.name: Centity
classes.doc: One spawned centity: `this` in the centity's script, and what `nf.centities.spawn`, `nf.centities.get` and `nf.centities.all` return. A handle stays valid as long as the instance exists; after it's removed its methods return `nil` or `false` rather than erroring.

events.name: spawn
events.doc: Once, when the instance is first put into the world, after its script's body has run: not when it comes back after a restart or a reload. A script's body runs every time it starts; this is for what happens only once.

events.name: remove
events.doc: The instance is being removed for good (`centity:remove()`, `/nf kill`). Its script then unloads (`nf.on("unload")`), and every handler on it and its nodes goes.

events.name: tick
events.doc: Every tick while the instance's chunk is loaded, or every `n` ticks with `{ every = n }`. Each instance falls on its own one of those `n` ticks, so a crowd of centities with `every = 4` spreads over four ticks rather than all running on one. A centity nobody listens to this on isn't ticked at all, and one whose handlers all have `every` is only called into on the ticks one is due.
events.example:
local angle = 0
this:on("tick", function()
  angle = (angle + 6) % 360
  this:node("blade"):set_rotation(vec3(0, angle, 0))
end)

events.name: click
events.doc: A player clicked one of its hitboxes: after the clicked node and the nodes above it, and before `nf.on("centity_click")`, unless one of them called `event:stop()`.
events.example:
this:on("click", function(event)
  this:play_animation("open")
  event.player:send_message("<gold>Opened")
end)

events.name: animation_start
events.doc: One of its animations started (`play_animation`), from the beginning.

events.name: animation_end
events.doc: An animation reached its end: a `once` clip has finished, a `hold` clip is holding its last pose. Looping clips never end.

events.name: chunk_load
events.doc: Its chunk came back into memory (someone came near), so it's ticking again.

events.name: chunk_unload
events.doc: Its chunk was unloaded (everyone went away): it stops ticking until `chunk_load`. Its handlers stay.

events.name: hit
